title: Campus Life & Making Friends
story_context: Ahmed has just arrived at Westfield University for orientation week. He is older than most students — 32 years old, having worked in warehouses and offices for a decade — but he earned his place here. He is nervous in a new way. Not about English, not about work ethic. About fitting in socially. He meets three people in the first two hours: Priya, an Indian-American sophomore who has been assigned as his orientation buddy; Jake, a 19-year-old from rural Georgia who seems to know everyone; and Zoe, a pre-med student from New Jersey who talks fast and moves faster.
objectives: Use tag questions naturally to open conversations and confirm shared understanding
Deploy casual discourse markers (actually, honestly, I mean, right?) to sound less stiff
Learn and use 10 core campus vocabulary words in realistic context
Start conversations with American college students using informal openers
target_phrases: It's your first day too, isn't it?
Honestly, I have no idea where I'm going.
What's your major, if you don't mind me asking?
I mean, it's a lot to take in, right?
Do you want to grab lunch after this?
We should hang out — I actually know some good spots.
I'm still figuring out the vibe here.

dialogue.title: Orientation Week
dialogue.context: Ahmed is standing outside the orientation hall with a campus map, clearly confused. Priya approaches him.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Hey — you look as lost as I did last year. First day?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Yes. It is my first day. I am looking for Building C, where the orientation session begins.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Ha! Yeah, Building C is kind of a disaster — it's actually behind the library, not in front. I'm Priya, by the way. I'm your orientation buddy.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: I am Ahmed. Thank you, Priya. I apologize — I was not aware that Building C was located behind the library. I should have reviewed the campus map more carefully.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Relax, everyone gets lost! Honestly, I got lost like three times my first week. What's your major?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Finance. We're practically in the same building all semester. We should hang out — I mean, study together and stuff.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: I would appreciate that. I mean — yes, that sounds good. I am still figuring out the vibe here, actually.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: The vibe is pretty chill once you get past the chaos. Oh — here comes Jake. Jake! Over here!

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Hey y'all! This must be the new guy. Ahmed, right? I'm Jake. You picked a heck of a semester to start, man — football season just kicked off.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: It is nice to meet you, Jake. Honestly, I do not know much about American football yet.

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: Don't even worry about it — you'll learn fast. Hey, do you want to grab lunch after orientation? There's a place off campus, best tacos you'll ever have.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Yes — I would like that. Do you want to come as well, Priya?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Obviously. I'm not missing tacos. Also, Ahmed — it's cool that you're being so formal, but you can just say 'yeah' sometimes. We won't judge.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Right. Yeah. Okay. I am working on it.

listening_exercises.transcript: So okay, orientation is basically a week of organized chaos. They're gonna throw a ton of information at you — where to get your ID, how to register for classes, dorm rules, dining plans, all of it. My advice? Don't stress about remembering everything. Just focus on meeting people. Honestly, the friends you make orientation week are usually the ones you keep. Like, your roommate situation might be random, but the people you grab food with, study with, complain about professors with — that's your crew.
listening_exercises.question: What does the speaker say is the most important thing to focus on during orientation week?
options: Memorizing where all the buildings are
Learning all the dorm rules immediately

listening_exercises.transcript: Ahmed: Hey, is this seat taken? Zoe: Go for it. You're in the BA program, right? I saw your name tag. I'm Zoe — pre-med, which basically means I live in the library. Ahmed: I am Ahmed. Pre-med sounds very demanding. Zoe: Oh it totally is. But honestly, I wouldn't trade it. What made you pick business admin? Ahmed: I have been working in business for about ten years, actually. I wanted the formal degree. Zoe: Wait — seriously? That's so cool. You've got real experience. Most of us here have no idea what actual work is like.
listening_exercises.question: Why does Zoe think Ahmed's situation is 'so cool'?
options: Because he is from another country
Because he has real work experience before college
Because he is older than her

listening_exercises.transcript: Making friends in college is different from making friends at work. At work, you share tasks. In college, you share everything — dining hall meals, late-night study sessions, stress about exams, weird roommate situations. The key is just showing up to things. Go to the orientation events even if they seem cheesy. Join one club you're actually interested in. Sit next to someone new in class. Ask questions. Americans, generally speaking, are pretty friendly to people who show genuine interest. A simple 'what's your major?' can start a friendship.
listening_exercises.question: According to the speaker, what is the key to making friends in college?
options: Having the same major as other students
Showing up to things and showing genuine interest

speaking_tasks.prompt: You are at orientation and you see someone standing alone looking at a campus map. Introduce yourself, ask about their major, and invite them to grab food later. Use at least two discourse markers and one tag question. Record for 30 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: Hey! You look a little lost — this campus is huge, isn't it? I'm Ahmed, by the way. Honestly, I've been walking in circles for twenty minutes. Are you in the BA program too? What's your major, if you don't mind me asking? I mean, I'm still figuring out the whole vibe here, but a few of us are going to grab tacos after this session — do you want to come?
sentence_starters: Hey! You look like you're also trying to figure out...
Honestly, I have no idea where...

speaking_tasks.prompt: Tell a classmate three things about yourself that are different from a typical 19-year-old freshman, but frame them positively and casually — not stiffly. Use informal language. Record for 35 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: So, yeah — I'm a little different from most freshmen. I mean, I'm 32, so I've actually been working for about ten years before coming here. I was in logistics and operations, actually. So the business stuff, I kind of know from the inside, right? But honestly, the social side — campus life, all of this — that's the part I'm still figuring out. I'm kind of learning a second language within English, if that makes sense. Like, professional English I've got. Casual American college English? That's a work in progress.
sentence_starters: So yeah, I'm kind of a non-traditional student...
Honestly, the thing that's different about me is...
I mean, I've got experience with...

writing_tasks.prompt: Write a short text message (4–6 lines) to someone you met at orientation, suggesting you hang out this weekend. Use informal language, contractions, and at least one casual opener or discourse marker. (40–60 words)
writing_tasks.example: Hey Priya! It was really cool meeting you at orientation. I'm still getting used to everything honestly. Did you want to maybe grab coffee this weekend and go over our schedules? I heard there's a good place near the library. Let me know if you're free Saturday morning!

writing_tasks.prompt: Write a short journal entry (80–100 words) about your first day on campus. Use a mix of formal observation and informal reflection — like a person who is naturally more formal learning to relax their voice.
writing_tasks.example:
Day 1 at Westfield University.

Honestly, I did not expect to feel this overwhelmed. I have managed teams, navigated airports in four countries, and sat in boardrooms — but today, surrounded by 19-year-olds who seem to know exactly how to exist here, I felt like the new kid.

I met Priya and Jake. Priya is organized and kind. Jake is impossible not to like. I also had my first American tacos.

I said 'yeah' once. Priya smiled like that was a big deal. Maybe it was.

I think I'm going to be okay.

grammar_focus.title: Tag Questions
grammar_focus.explanation: Tag questions are short questions added to the end of a statement. They confirm information or invite agreement. In American casual speech they are common and friendly — not challenging. Positive statement + negative tag: 'It's hot, isn't it?' Negative statement + positive tag: 'You haven't been here before, have you?'
examples: It's your first day, isn't it? (positive statement → negative tag)
You're in the BA program, aren't you? (confirming information)
This campus is huge, right? ('right' is the most casual all-purpose tag)
You haven't found the dining hall yet, have you? (negative → positive tag)
We're in the same orientation group, aren't we? (building connection)

practice.sentence: You haven't registered for classes yet, ___ you?
We're in the same lecture hall, ___ we?

grammar_focus.title: Discourse Markers in Casual Speech
grammar_focus.explanation: Discourse markers are words that organize spoken language and signal your attitude. They do not carry heavy meaning — they make speech sound natural and connected. 'Honestly' signals openness. 'Actually' signals a correction or surprising fact. 'I mean' signals clarification. 'Right?' invites agreement. Used too rarely, speech sounds stiff; used well, it sounds fluent.
examples: Honestly, I got lost three times my first week. (signals candid admission)
Actually, Building C is behind the library. (signals correction)
I mean, it's a lot to process, right? (signals clarification + invites agreement)
We should hang out — actually, I know some good spots. (signals addition)
Honestly, I was nervous too — I mean, everyone is. (combines two markers)

practice.sentence: ___, I have no idea where the library is. (signals candid admission)
___, the exam is on Thursday, not Friday. (signals correction)
I mean, it's a lot to take in, ___? (invites agreement)

grammar_focus.title: Casual Invitations: Do you want to / We should / Let's
grammar_focus.explanation: Americans invite each other using soft, low-pressure structures. 'Do you want to grab coffee?' is friendlier than 'Would you like to have coffee with me?' 'We should hang out' is an open invitation without a specific commitment. 'Let's grab lunch' is direct and inclusive. These structures reduce social risk — they are easy to accept or decline without awkwardness.
examples: Do you want to grab lunch after this? (casual, low-pressure invitation)
We should hang out this weekend. (open-ended, no specific pressure)
Let's find the dining hall together. (inclusive, immediate)
Do you want to catch up later and compare schedules? (practical + social)
We should study together sometime. ('sometime' keeps it open)

practice.sentence: ___ you want to grab coffee before class?
We ___ hang out sometime — I know a good spot.

vocabulary.example: Orientation week helped me learn where all the buildings are.

vocabulary.example: Her major is Finance, so she takes a lot of math classes.

vocabulary.example: My dorm room is small but it's close to all my classes.

vocabulary.definition: a person you share a room or apartment with

vocabulary.definition: to spend time with someone in a relaxed, informal way
vocabulary.example: Do you want to hang out after class and get coffee?

vocabulary.example: Let's grab lunch before the afternoon session.

cultural_notes: Orientation week at American universities is highly social — the unspoken purpose is making friends, not just learning logistics. Attending events and being visible matters more than the content of the events.
Americans tend to ask 'What's your major?' as the first social question to a college student. It's the college equivalent of 'What do you do?' — a quick way to find common ground.

Saying 'we should hang out sometime' or 'let's grab coffee' is often a genuine but open invitation with no fixed plan. The follow-up message is what actually creates the plan — the initial phrase signals friendliness.

Being older or non-traditional in college is increasingly common and generally respected. Sharing work experience honestly (without being arrogant) creates interest and connection rather than awkwardness.
Discourse markers like 'honestly' and 'I mean' are not filler words to eliminate — they are social signals. Removing them all makes speech sound cold or overly formal to American ears.
